docs.title: oboromi
docs.text:
This is the documentation of oboromi, an early Nintendo Switch 2 emulator written in Rust. It builds on the CPU, service, GPU and front-end foundations laid by its maintainer and contributors. The project's own AArch64 programs run through the loader, kernel, stand-in services, audio renderer and GPU path.

The project's test programs hand the emulated Ampere GPU small programs called shaders, for example one that computes the colour of each pixel of a sky. Those shaders are NVIDIA machine code. The emulator rewrites them into SPIR-V, the shader format of the cross-vendor graphics API Vulkan. Then an Intel, AMD or NVIDIA card in a PC can run them.

The Julia demo runs on the emulator and dispatches Ampere machine code, translated to SPIR-V, on an Intel laptop GPU.

Start here For Architecture map One picture of the whole emulator, and which page answers what Decision records The big design choices, each explained in plain words first Glossary Every GPU term the pages use, with one plain sentence and an example SM86 instruction table (PDF) The desktop Ampere instruction encodings used by the translator, generated from NVIDIA's table

docs.title: Build a program
docs.text: The triangle is the smallest of the project's own test programs that runs on the emulator. Its source is guest/src/bin/triangle.rs.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
These versions are known to work:

Tool Version Rust and Cargo 1.92.0 Rust target aarch64-unknown-none Rust LLVM objcopy 21.1.3 glslangValidator 16.2.0 Mesa NAK 25.2.7 CUDA tools for the NVIDIA path 13.1

Install the Rust target and LLVM tools:

rustup target add aarch64-unknown-none
rustup component add llvm-tools
./demos/assets/fetch.sh

The build runs on a Linux x86-64 host. The asset fetch is needed because the crate's build script prepares data shared by all its binaries.

docs.title: Build the CPU program
docs.text:
The program is no_std and starts at _start. It asks sm for services, then sends IPC requests to nvdrv and vi to allocate GPU memory, submit work and present a frame. Programs that need controls or sound use the same path to reach hid and audren.

cargo build --release --target aarch64-unknown-none \
  --manifest-path guest/Cargo.toml --target-dir target/guest --bin triangle
objcopy="$(rustc --print sysroot)/lib/rustlib/$(rustc -vV | sed -n 's/^host: //p')/bin/rust-objcopy"
"$objcopy" -O binary target/guest/aarch64-unknown-none/release/triangle triangle.nro

docs.title: Build shaders
docs.text:
The repository's exact fixtures come from GLSL compiled through the NVIDIA driver on an NVIDIA card. For a local build, Mesa's NAK compiler produces the shader header and SM86 SASS:

TMPDIR="$HOME/.cache/tmp" \
NAK_OFFLINE=/path/to/mesa-25.2.7/build/src/nouveau/compiler/nak-offline \
NVDISASM=/usr/local/cuda-13.1/bin/nvdisasm \
BINDINGS=u1,s2 tools/nak-compile.sh demos/shaders/post.vert sass-out

BINDINGS is the descriptor shim: u is a uniform buffer, s a sampler, b a storage buffer and a an acceleration structure. Omit it for shaders without bindings. Put the resulting .bin files under core/tests/fixtures/driver-shaders; programs such as guest/src/bin/dungeon.rs copy them to mapped GPU memory with shader(address, bytes). The triangle is smaller and writes its built-in shader bytes through scene::triangle_scene instead.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Capture one frame from the NRO:

cargo run --release -p oboromi-core --example capture -- \
  ./triangle.nro --seconds 1 --fps 1 --out "$HOME/.cache/oboromi-triangle"

For parity checks, use exact mode and compare the CPU path with the reference renderer:

OBOROMI_EXACT=1 cargo test -p oboromi-core guest_triangle_end_to_end -- --nocapture
cargo test -p oboromi-core nak_compiled_triangle_matches_driver -- --nocapture

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• NAK does not compile ray queries; use the NVIDIA driver path for them.
  • Speed hacks are enabled by default. Set OBOROMI_EXACT=1 for exact results.
  • The supported host is Linux x86-64.
  • The loader accepts NRO and flat AArch64 images, including an optional NRO RomFS. It does not load retail game formats.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
A game talks to its GPU through command words in memory and small programs called shaders. Each piece on that path has its own name. For example, to draw a triangle the game writes a command list and points the GPU at it. The GPU then runs a shader for every covered pixel.

flowchart LR
    GPFIFO["GPFIFO<br/>Queue of pointers to command lists"] --> PB["Pushbuffer<br/>One command list in memory"] --> M["Methods<br/>Single register writes"]
    M --> C3["3D class<br/>Drawing settings: shaders, constants, textures"]
    M --> CC["Compute class<br/>Compute launches, described by a QMD"]
    C3 --> SASS["SASS<br/>NVIDIA shader machine code"]
    CC --> SASS
    SASS -->|"Translator"| SPIRV["SPIR-V<br/>The shader format Vulkan runs"]

How a game's commands lead to shader code a PC's GPU can run.

docs.title: Chips and code formats
docs.text: Term What it is Example GPU The graphics chip: many small cores running the same program on many pixels or numbers at once. Shading every pixel of a frame in parallel. Emulated system, PC The emulated system is the Switch 2 model and its RAM; the PC runs oboromi. An emulated address points into console RAM. Shader A small program the GPU runs once per vertex, pixel or work item. A pixel shader that returns one pixel's colour. SASS NVIDIA's native GPU machine code, the instructions the chip really executes. FADD R0, R1, R2 adds two floats; on SM86 each instruction is a 128-bit word. SM86 The instruction set of NVIDIA's Ampere desktop chips, used as the translator's target. An RTX 3090 runs SM86 code. SM88 NVIDIA's disassembler target for the Switch 2 GPU; its bundled encoding table equals SM86's. nvdisasm --binary SM88 accepts the SM88 target. Ampere NVIDIA's GPU generation shared by desktop cards and the Switch 2. RTX 30 series cards are Ampere. T239 The Switch 2's system-on-chip: ARM CPU cores plus an Ampere GPU called GA10F. The main chip inside every Switch 2. GA102 The desktop Ampere chip the reference results are recorded on. RTX 3090 and RTX A6000 are GA102 cards. Silicon Real hardware, as opposed to an emulator or a CPU-based driver. "matches silicon" means an RTX 3090 gave the same bytes. SPIR-V The binary shader format Vulkan accepts, like bytecode for GPUs. The translator writes one SPIR-V module per shader. Module One SPIR-V program, ready to hand to a Vulkan driver. The translated Julia demo shader. Translator oboromi's code that rewrites SASS into SPIR-V. core/src/gpu/sm86. Encoding class One row of NVIDIA's instruction table: a bit pattern plus its fields. An add with a register operand and one with a constant are two classes. Handler The translator function that emits SPIR-V for one instruction family. The FADD handler emits a float add. Opcode The name of an instruction. IMAD is integer multiply-add.

docs.title: How commands reach the GPU
docs.text: Term What it is Example Channel One stream of commands from a program to the GPU. A game's renderer usually owns one. GPFIFO A ring of small entries, each pointing at a pushbuffer and giving its length. The game appends one entry per batch of commands. Pushbuffer A list of 32-bit command words in emulated RAM: a header word, then data words. "set viewport width to 1920" is one header and one data word. Method One register write to a GPU engine, named by its register offset. Writing the vertex count before a draw. Class A GPU engine's set of registers, identified by a number. 0xC797 is the Ampere 3D engine, 0xC7C0 compute, 0xC76F the channel. Subchannel One of eight slots a channel binds a class into, so each header can pick an engine. Subchannel 0 holds the 3D class after SET_OBJECT. SET_OBJECT The channel method that binds a class to a subchannel. Sent once at the start of a command stream. Draw trigger The method write that means "draw now with the current settings". DRAW_VERTEX_ARRAY_BEGIN_END_INSTANCE_FIRST. Snapshot A frozen copy of the GPU settings at the moment of a draw or launch. DrawSnapshot holds the viewport the draw used. Semaphore A memory word the GPU writes or waits on, to tell the CPU how far it got. A release writes a counter when a frame is done. Syncpoint The Switch's hardware counter for the same job, managed by the OS. The display waits on one before showing a frame. Report A value the GPU writes to memory on request. A counter or timestamp after a draw. MME, MME64 A small macro processor in the GPU that expands one call into many method writes. One macro call that sets up a whole draw. QMD Queue meta data: a block in emulated RAM describing one compute launch. Grid size, threads per group, program address, constant buffers. Dispatch One compute launch: run a program over a grid of threads. One dispatch per frame of the Julia demo.

docs.title: Shaders and their data
docs.text: Term What it is Example Stage Which step of drawing a shader belongs to. Vertex, fragment or compute. Vertex shader Runs once per corner of a triangle and computes where it lands on screen. Multiplying a position by the camera matrix. Fragment shader Runs once per covered pixel and computes its colour; also called a pixel shader. Sampling a texture and returning the colour. Compute shader A shader not tied to drawing, run over a grid of threads for general work. The Julia set demo. SPH Shader program header: a block before a graphics program naming its stage, inputs and outputs. "vertex stage, writes position and one colour". IMAP, OMAP The SPH's input and output maps: which attributes a shader reads and writes. OMAP bit for "writes generic attribute 0". Attribute A per-vertex value passed between stages. Position, colour or texture coordinate. Interpolation Blending a vertex value across a triangle's pixels; "flat" means no blending. A colour fading from one corner to another. cbuf Constant buffer: a small read-only table of numbers the game hands the shader. The camera matrix, read as c[bank][offset]. Bank Which of a shader's constant buffers an access names. Bank 0 carries launch data in compute, such as the grid size. Global memory The GPU's view of main memory, read and written by address. LDG loads from it, STG stores to it. Shared memory A small fast scratch area shared by the threads of one workgroup. Threads swapping partial sums. Local memory Per-thread scratch memory for values that do not fit in registers. A large per-thread array. Register A named per-thread variable inside the GPU core. R0 to R253; RZ always reads zero. Predicate A one-bit register that decides whether an instruction runs. @P0 FADD adds only where P0 is true. Uniform datapath Per-warp registers holding one value shared by all its threads. UR0 to UR62 and predicates UP0 to UP6. pc Program counter: the position of the next instruction. A branch sets the pc to its target. Basic block A run of instructions entered only at the top and left only at the bottom. The body of a loop without inner branches. Attribute space The address range an instruction uses to name an attribute. Position sits at 0x70.

docs.title: How the GPU runs threads
docs.text: Term What it is Example Thread, invocation, lane One running copy of a shader; Vulkan says invocation, and a lane is a thread's slot in a warp. The thread shading one pixel. Warp A team of threads that runs one instruction stream in lockstep. NVIDIA warps are 32 threads. Subgroup Vulkan's name for a warp; its width depends on the device. lavapipe's subgroups are 8 wide. Workgroup A group of threads that can share memory and wait for each other; CUDA calls it a block. 256 threads working on one tile of an image. Divergence Threads of one warp taking different sides of a branch. Pixels inside and outside a circle. Reconvergence The point where diverged threads join up again. The end of an if-else. BSSY, BSYNC The SM86 instruction pair marking where diverged threads of a warp join again. BSSY before an if, BSYNC after it. Barrier A point every thread of a group must reach before any goes on. BAR before reading what others wrote to shared memory. Collective An instruction where threads of a warp exchange values. VOTE asks which threads have a condition; SHFL reads a teammate's register. Structured control flow SPIR-V's rule that branches must form nested loops and ifs, with no free jumps. No goto into the middle of a loop.

docs.title: Textures
docs.text: Term What it is Example Texture An image a shader reads with filtering. A brick wall image on a model. Sampler The settings for reading a texture: edge wrapping, filtering, level of detail. Repeat at the edges, smooth between pixels. TIC Texture image control: a header describing one texture's format, size, layout, address and mip levels. One 32-byte entry per texture. TSC Texture sampler control: an entry holding one sampler's settings. One 32-byte entry per sampler. Pool A table of TIC or TSC entries in emulated RAM. A game's texture pool with hundreds of headers. Handle A cbuf word that picks one TIC entry and one TSC entry. Low 20 bits pick the texture, top 12 bits the sampler. Mip level A smaller copy of the same texture, used when it appears far away. A 512 pixel texture with 256, 128 and smaller copies. LOD Level of detail: which mip level a read uses. LOD 0 is full size. Format How a pixel's bytes are laid out. A8B8G8R8 is four 8-bit channels; BC1, BC3, BC7 are compressed. sRGB A colour encoding matching how screens show brightness, decoded to linear before maths. Most photos and base-colour textures. Pitch-linear Plain rows of pixels, one after another. A screenshot in memory. Block-linear NVIDIA's tiled layout that keeps nearby pixels close in memory. Most textures a game uploads. GOB Group of bytes: the small tile block-linear layouts are built from. 64 bytes wide and 8 rows high. Deswizzle Reorder tiled pixels back into plain rows. Turning a block-linear texture into a Vulkan image. Surface An image a shader writes pixel by pixel instead of sampling; Vulkan calls it a storage image. SUST stores one pixel. Render target The image a draw writes its pixels into. A colour image plus an optional depth image. Index buffer A list of vertex numbers saying which vertices form each triangle, so shared corners are stored once. A square as four vertices and six indices. Instancing Drawing the same mesh many times in one call, with per-copy data such as position. A thousand particles in one draw. Blending Mixing a new pixel's colour with the one already in the image. A see-through window over a wall. Window origin Whether screen y counts from the top or the bottom row of the image. OpenGL-style games count from the bottom. Depth Per-pixel distance, used to hide what is behind. A wall in front of a door.

docs.title: Tensor cores
docs.text: Term What it is Example Tensor core A unit that multiplies small matrices in one instruction. AI inference and upscaling use them. HMMA, IMMA Matrix multiply-accumulate on tensor cores, for half-precision floats and for integers. One HMMA computes D = A × B + C across a warp. DMMA, BMMA The same for double-precision floats and for single bits. DMMA for scientific maths. LDSM, MOVM Load and rearrange matrix pieces for tensor instructions. Loading a tile from shared memory. Matrix fragment The part of a matrix one thread holds. A few elements of row 3 of A. TF32 A reduced-precision float format tensor cores use for speed. 32 bits of storage, fewer mantissa bits used. Truncation Dropping low bits instead of rounding them. 1.27 truncated to one decimal is 1.2. IEEE order Adding numbers one at a time, rounding after each step, as standard float rules do. ((a + b) + c) + d.

docs.title: Vulkan
docs.text: Term What it is Example Vulkan The cross-vendor API programs use to drive a GPU. The same code runs on Intel, AMD and NVIDIA. ICD Installable client driver: the library that gives Vulkan a device. lavapipe's ICD file. Queue Where a program submits work to the GPU. One queue that takes both graphics and compute. Command buffer A recorded list of GPU commands submitted in one go. "bind pipeline, dispatch, copy back". Fence A flag the GPU sets when submitted work finishes, so the CPU can wait. Waiting for a dispatch before reading its output. Pipeline A compiled bundle of shaders plus fixed settings, needed before any draw or dispatch. Vertex shader, fragment shader, vertex layout and colour format. Dynamic state Settings that can change per draw without building a new pipeline. Viewport and cull mode. Dynamic rendering Drawing straight into images, without Vulkan's older render pass objects. One call names the colour and depth images. Descriptor A small record telling a shader where one buffer or image is. "binding 33 is this buffer". Binding A numbered slot a shader reads a resource from; the host plugs a buffer or image into it. Binding 9 holds the global memory window. Descriptor set A group of bindings plugged in together. Vertex and compute resources use set 0; fragment resources use set 1. Uniform buffer A small read-only buffer behind a binding. A game's cbuf. Storage buffer, SSBO A large buffer a shader can read and write. The global memory window. std140 Vulkan's layout rule for uniform buffers, which pads each array element to 16 bytes. Why cbufs are declared as uvec4 arrays. uvec4 Four 32-bit unsigned integers, 16 bytes in total. One row of a cbuf array. Resource list The bindings a translated module declares, with what each one holds. "binding 1 is cbuf 0, binding 36 is the texture at cbuf 0 offset 0x10". Validation layer A Vulkan debug layer that reports misuse of the API. Catching an image used in the wrong layout. spirv-val The Khronos tool that checks a SPIR-V module is valid. It rejected a compute shader that used OpKill. lavapipe Mesa's Vulkan driver that runs on the CPU, also called llvmpipe. The device in CI. DontUnroll A SPIR-V hint asking the driver not to copy a loop body out. Keeps a four-pass loop as a loop. Inlining A compiler pasting a function's body into every caller. A helper function vanishing from the compiled code. Register spill Moving values to slower memory when a program needs more registers than the core has. Intel spilling in the tensor loops. Readback Copying results from GPU memory back to CPU memory. Reading a frame's pixels after a draw. Denormal A tiny float close to zero that some hardware flushes to zero. 1e-40 as a 32-bit float. NaN "not a number", the float result of an invalid operation. 0.0 / 0.0.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Term What it is Example VA, PA GPU virtual address, which shaders use, and physical address, where the bytes sit in emulated RAM. One VA can be repointed to another PA. Page The fixed-size chunk the address map works in. 64 KiB here. Page map The table that turns GPU virtual pages into physical RAM pages. PageMap in memory.rs. Remap Pointing a GPU address at different memory. A game moving a vertex buffer. Aliasing Two addresses sharing the same memory. A texture that is also a render target. Mirror A PC-side copy of an emulated buffer, kept for Vulkan. The vertex buffer copy a draw reads. Generation A counter stamped on each page write, so a copy can tell it is stale. A mirror refreshes when its pages' generation moved. Coherence Keeping all copies of the same data in agreement. The CPU seeing the pixels a draw wrote. Global memory window One storage buffer holding the emulated memory range a program can touch. The output image of the gradient program. Memory descriptor An extra policy word the compiler attaches to some loads and stores; it is not part of the address. LDG.E desc[UR4][R2.64].

docs.title: The rest of the emulator
docs.text: Term What it is Example Dynarmic The default AArch64 JIT backend. It runs the included demos unless exact mode is selected. Unicorn The comparison and exact AArch64 backend, built on QEMU's CPU core. OBOROMI_CPU=unicorn selects it. QEMU The open-source machine emulator whose CPU core Unicorn reuses. It also runs whole ARM Linux systems. Cortex-A78C The Arm CPU core in the Switch 2's chip. Eight of them in the T239. switchbrew The community wiki that documents the Switch's system calls, services and hardware. Its NV services page. libnx The homebrew library for writing Switch programs. The request encoder follows its layout. AArch64 The 64-bit ARM instruction set the Switch 2's CPU runs. The game's main code. FFI Foreign function interface: the Rust functions the C++ Qt window calls. ffi.rs. HLE High-level emulation: writing a firmware service's behaviour instead of running its code. Answering a "get time" call directly. Service An OS process a game talks to. nvdrv is the GPU driver service, vi the display service. HIPC The Switch's message format for calling services. A header plus arguments in a buffer. SVC Supervisor call: a system call into the Switch kernel. Mapping memory. Ioctl A control call into a driver. An nvdrv call that allocates GPU memory. nvmap, host1x The Switch's GPU memory allocator and its sync and DMA unit. nvmap hands out buffer handles. NSO, NRO Switch executable file formats. A game's main program is an NSO. Loader The code that places an executable in memory and starts it. The NRO loader starts an included demo image. Session An open connection from a game to one service. A session with nvdrv. Handle A number the kernel gives a program to name something it opened. The session handle SendSyncRequest takes. Port A named address a program connects to in order to open a session. The port named nvdrv. IPC Inter-process communication: one program sending a message to another. A game asking the display service for a layer. IPC buffer A small per-thread memory area that holds the request and then the reply. The request bytes for SendSyncRequest. CMIF The command layer on top of HIPC: a magic word, a command id and arguments. SFCI, then command 1, then the ioctl number. Transfer memory Emulated memory a program lends to a service. The audio renderer's work buffer. Driver fence A sync counter value a program waits on to know its GPU work finished. The fence SubmitGpfifo returns. Binder The display's messaging layer, inherited from Android, for handing over frames. QueueBuffer through IHOSBinderDriver. Turn lock The lock that lets either the CPU or the GPU use emulated RAM, never both. The GPU takes it before a draw. Write hook A CPU-backend callback for stores to a watched range. Marking pages the GPU must refresh.

docs.title: Tools, tests and references
docs.text:
Term What it is Example nvdisasm NVIDIA's disassembler; the decoder is generated from the instruction table it carries. Turning a 128-bit word into FADD R0, R1, R2. nvcc NVIDIA's CUDA compiler. nvcc -arch=sm_86 -cubin kernel.cu. CUDA NVIDIA's way of writing general GPU programs in C++. A kernel that adds two arrays. Kernel A CUDA program launched over a grid of threads. The mul-add test kernel. cubin An ELF file holding compiled CUDA kernels for one SM version. kernels.cubin. libcuda NVIDIA's driver library that runs CUDA programs on its cards. libcuda.so.1. Capture One recording of an instruction run on a real card: inputs, instruction, outputs. An integer add with its result registers. Fixture A stored test case, here usually a capture. One line of sm86-thread.jsonl. Scoreboard test A test that replays every capture and fails on any unlisted mismatch. fixtures_match_silicon. Seed kernel A small compiled CUDA program used as a carrier for one patched instruction. cuda-seed.cu. Ryujinx An open-source Switch 1 emulator whose GPU code is a reference. Its texture size calculator. NAK Mesa's open-source shader compiler for NVIDIA GPUs. Its shader header layout. Open-gpu-doc NVIDIA's public hardware headers. clc797.h, the 3D class registers. Mesa The open-source graphics driver stack on Linux. It ships lavapipe. glTF A standard 3D model file format. The BoomBox sample model. PBR Physically based rendering: lighting that follows real material behaviour. Metal and rough surfaces lit by one light. Voice One playing sound in the audio renderer. A footstep sample with its volume and pitch. Mix A bus that voices or other mixes add into. All sound effects together. Sink Where the audio renderer's final sound goes. The device sink, the speakers. ADPCM A compressed sample format the Switch's audio uses. Music stored at a quarter of its PCM size. Biquad A small audio filter that cuts or boosts some frequencies. A low-pass to muffle a sound behind a wall. Ray query A shader asking "what does this ray hit first?" against the scene. A shadow ray from a pixel towards the light. Acceleration structure A search tree over a scene's triangles that makes ray queries fast. Built once per model, then queried per pixel.

Sources: core/src/gpu/{fifo,threed,texture,engine}.rs, core/src/gpu/compute_class.rs on gpu/qmd-dispatch, NVIDIA's open-gpu-doc class headers.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text:
A decision record, or ADR, explains one design choice: the problem, the choice, and what it costs. Each one opens with a short "In plain words" section, then the details. For example, ADR-0004 explains why emulated RAM is the one true copy of all data.

ADR Decision 0001 Every shader finds its data in one fixed table of numbered slots 0002 Game memory reaches a shader through one window buffer 0003 Threads that take different branches run in turns 0004 Emulated RAM is the one true copy; host copies check a write counter 0005 Matrix sums copy the chip exactly, written as small loops 0006 GPU commands run one after another, each draw with frozen settings 0007 Use the desktop instruction table for the T239 target 0008 Real chips are the reference, known differences are listed per device

Each record follows the MADR template and names its component in the front matter.

docs.title: Every shader finds its data in a fixed table of numbered slots
In plain words
docs.text: A Vulkan shader cannot follow a pointer to its data. Instead it reads from numbered slots, and before each run the host plugs a buffer or an image into each slot. Think of a patch panel: the shader asks for a socket by number and reads whatever is plugged in there. We fixed the socket numbers once, for every shader, so the host always knows what goes where.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: A translated shader needs several kinds of data: our own helper values, the game's constant tables, the game's main memory, and any number of textures. Compute shaders and drawing shaders must agree on which slot holds what. A vertex shader and a pixel shader drawing together may each want their own buffer in the same slot.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Vulkan calls a slot a binding and a group of slots a descriptor set. Compute and vertex shaders use set 0. Pixel shaders use set 1, with the same slot numbers. Each set holds these slots:

Binding Vulkan kind Holds 0 Uniform buffer: small, read-only Our helper values, today the start address of the memory window; never game data 1 to 32 Uniform buffers The game's constant buffers 0 to 31, all the banks a stage has 33 Storage buffer: large, read-write The window onto the game's main memory, see ADR-0002 34, 35 Storage buffers Register values in and out, for tests only 36 and up Image slots Textures and writable images, numbered in the order the shader first uses them

A constant buffer, or cbuf, is a small read-only table of numbers the game hands the shader, such as the camera matrix. Vulkan's layout rule for uniform buffers, std140, pads each array element to a fixed width. A uvec4 is exactly that width, so each cbuf is declared as a uvec4 array and no space is wasted.

Layout fact Value std140 array element Padded to 16 bytes uvec4 Four 32-bit words, 16 bytes

Two texture reads whose handle comes from the same cbuf word share one slot. A shader declares only the slots it uses. That list, its resource list, tells the host exactly what to plug in.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• One piece of host code, Descriptors, plugs in data for compute and for both drawing stages.
  • Our helper values can never be confused with what the game put in its first constant buffer.
  • A draw's vertex and pixel shaders can read different buffers through the same cbuf slot, because each has its own set.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Every draw binds two sets instead of one, and the host must keep them apart.
  • Shaders that pick a texture by a run-time index will need arrays of slots next to this layout.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
Checked by spirv-val on every module, the Vulkan validation layer on dispatch and draw, and the texture tests that bind several images at once.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/mod.rs, core/src/gpu/compute.rs.

docs.title: Game memory reaches a shader through one window buffer
In plain words
docs.text: Game shaders read memory by address, like a pointer in C. A Vulkan shader cannot use those addresses, because they point into the emulated console, not into the PC. So before each run the host copies the stretch of game memory the program may touch into one buffer, the window. The shader turns each game address into a position in that window by subtracting the window's start.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: SASS loads and stores use the game's own GPU addresses. Vulkan shaders cannot follow those. Vulkan's own shader pointers, buffer device addresses, point into host memory and know nothing about the game's address map.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
All main memory a run touches, called global memory, is one storage buffer at binding 33. A storage buffer is a large buffer a shader can read and write.

The PC looks the game's address range up in the page map, the table from GPU addresses to emulated RAM. It copies that range into one buffer and stores the window's start address in the helper slot, binding 0. For a compute launch from a command list, the range is all mapped emulated RAM. After the run, the pages the program changed are written back.

Window fact Value Start address Rounded down to a 16-byte boundary Widest access 128 bits Window for a launch from a command list All mapped emulated RAM, at most 4 GiB

A translated LDG (load from global memory) or STG (store) subtracts the start and indexes the buffer. An address outside mapped memory fails with an error. Buffer device addresses are not used.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• One rule covers every load, store and atomic, at any width the chip has.
  • A missing mapping is a clear error instead of a read of random memory.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• The window must hold every byte the program might touch, so the first launch copies all mapped memory to the card; later launches only copy pages that changed.
  • Some loads carry a memory descriptor, an extra policy word from the compiler, and it must not be added to the address.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The compiled mul-add kernel and the gradient program match the real card through this window. The engine test runs the gradient kernel from a QMD launch and finds its output in emulated RAM. The memory tests cover remaps.

Sources: core/src/gpu/memory.rs window, core/src/gpu/sm86/access.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/harness.rs run_grid.

docs.title: In plain words
docs.text: The GPU runs threads in teams called warps. When teammates take different branches, the real chip parks some, runs the others, and joins them back later. Some instructions make teammates swap values, so they must be at the same place at the same time. We run such programs in turns: each turn, the teammates furthest behind take one step while the rest wait. It is like a tour group where the stragglers always walk next, so everyone meets at every stop.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The translator runs each thread as a loop over its own program counter, the pc. Collectives, instructions where teammates swap values such as VOTE and SHFL, need every thread to reach the same Vulkan barrier together. So does BAR, the chip's own barrier. With threads at different pcs that is undefined behaviour, and votes by part of a warp could not be reproduced.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• Rebuild the game's jumps as nested Vulkan loops and ifs.
  • Use only Vulkan's subgroups, its own name for warps.
  • Keep the pc loop, and run it in turns across the whole thread group.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Keep the pc loop. A program with collectives or BAR moves every thread of its group, the workgroup, together. Each turn the group votes for the lowest pc any thread waits at. Threads at that pc run one step, and the rest sit out with their memory writes masked.

BSSY and BSYNC, the chip's "rejoin here" markers, are tracked per thread. BAR arrivals are counted per barrier until all the required threads arrive. Programs without collectives keep the free per-thread loop. Swapping values through shared memory is the one method on every device.

Device fact Value NVIDIA warp width 32 threads Subgroup width on lavapipe 8 threads

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Votes, shuffles and barriers after a branch match the real chip, including votes by part of a warp.
  • It runs on lavapipe, whose subgroups are narrower than a warp.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Programs with collectives pay a vote and a barrier on every step.
  • Whether a thread spinning in a wait loop ever lets the others move is not verified.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The warp scoreboard passes on Intel and lavapipe, and tests cover branches of unequal length, nested markers and early exit.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/mod.rs translate_program, core/src/gpu/sm86/warp.rs.

docs.title: Emulated RAM is the one true copy of all data
In plain words
docs.text: Vulkan cannot read the emulated console's RAM directly, so the emulator keeps PC-side copies of game data. Copies can go stale: the game might move a buffer, change it from the CPU, or draw into memory it later reads as a texture. So emulated RAM is the only truth. Every copy remembers where it came from and when, and every draw writes its pixels back to RAM before it returns. Think of a shared master file: anyone holding a printout checks the date before using it.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The engine keeps host copies of game data: buffer copies, the images draws paint into, and translated shaders. The game can repoint a GPU address, write a buffer from the CPU, or draw into memory it later reads. A host copy must never show what the game's memory does not hold.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Emulated RAM is the one source of truth. Every PC-side copy is keyed by physical ranges, where the bytes really sit. It is not keyed by GPU virtual address, which the game can point elsewhere.

A MemoryTracker stamps each page write with a global counter, the generation, and who wrote it, CPU or GPU. A copy refreshes when the counter on its pages moved.

Every draw writes its render target, the image it painted, back to emulated RAM before submit returns. It also records the counter it left. If the target's pages changed since, by the CPU or a clear, the next draw loads it from RAM first. Textures follow the same rule, so a texture that was drawn into shows its latest draw.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Moved and shared memory are right by construction, and drawing into a texture then reading it is just a read of RAM.
  • A CPU read after submit always sees what the GPU wrote.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Every draw pays for copying its pixels back, which is fine for demos but too slow for a game at full speed.
  • A small write refreshes a whole page.
  • Depth targets are not written back yet, so a depth target must be cleared before its first draw.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The engine tests repoint a vertex buffer address between draws and check the next draw follows it. They also sample a target as a texture after drawing into it, and load a clear that no draw used.

Sources: core/src/gpu/memory.rs, core/src/gpu/engine.rs.

docs.title: Matrix sums copy the chip exactly, written as small loops
docs.text: Exact mode uses this decision. The default selects the cooperative tensor speed hack.

docs.title: In plain words
docs.text: Tensor cores multiply small matrices in one instruction. The real chip adds up the products its own way: in groups, with the lowest bits cut off instead of rounded. Normal float maths gives slightly different last bits, so we copied the chip's method exactly. Written out naively, that makes shaders so big that drivers take seconds to compile them. So we wrote it as small loops and told the driver not to unroll them.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The chip sums HMMA products, the half-precision matrix multiply-add, in groups lined up to the largest exponent and truncated. It does not add them one at a time with rounding, as standard IEEE float rules do. A chain of standard fused multiply-adds disagreed with the recordings from a real card. The exact method, written out in full, made each HMMA a shader drivers were slow to compile. Wrapping it in one SPIR-V function did not help, because both drivers inlined it, pasting it back into every caller.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Implement the chip's method exactly:

Step Rule Grouping Eight products per group along k, four for TF32 (a reduced-precision float) Alignment Every term lined up to the largest exponent Truncation Bits below that are dropped, not rounded Sum An exact integer sum, turned back into a float by truncation .F16 results Each group rounds to a half-precision float Inf and NaN Standard float rules, applied to only those special terms Code shape Four loops, each marked DontUnroll

The inputs are loaded once into a per-thread array. DontUnroll is a SPIR-V hint that tells the driver to keep a loop as a loop. Loop state lives in plain per-thread variables, not in phi values, the compiler's merge points at the top of a loop.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• The tensor tests match the real chip bit for bit on Intel and lavapipe.
  • Shaders with tensor instructions compile fast again on both drivers.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Intel runs out of registers in this form, so warm runs are a little slower than standard float maths.
  • The speed relies on drivers honouring DontUnroll, which is checked on Intel and lavapipe only.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The tensor silicon scoreboard and the per-instruction compile timings in textures and tensors.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/tensor.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/tensor.rs.

docs.title: GPU commands run one after another, each draw with frozen settings
In plain words
docs.text: A program's command list mixes settings changes, draws, constant updates, clears and "tell the CPU I'm done" signals. Their order matters, but the PC's graphics card runs on its own clock. So we process a whole command list before returning. Every draw gets a frozen copy of its settings, everything runs in list order, and the results are in emulated RAM when the call returns. It is like a cashier who rings up each item before taking the next: slower than a busy kitchen, but never out of order.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: A pushbuffer, the program's command list, interleaves state writes, draws, constant buffer updates, clears and semaphore releases, the GPU's "got this far" signals. The order they take effect in matters, and a host GPU queue runs on its own clock. Nintendo's OS would wait on fences, the host's done-flags, or syncpoints, the Switch's hardware counters; oboromi does not emulate that OS.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Pusher::submit reads the GPFIFO, the queue of command lists, to the end and returns an ordered list of events. The 3D class keeps the raw register words. At each draw it copies what that draw needs into a frozen DrawSnapshot.

LOAD_CONSTANT_BUFFER, which updates a constant table, is an event in the same list. So are compute launches, clears, reports, semaphore releases and acquires. They therefore apply in command order.

The engine runs each event before the next, and Gpu::submit returns once every draw is back in emulated RAM. An acquire must already be met when it is reached, since nothing else runs that could release it. There are no macros (MME) yet, and no overlap of GPU work.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Ordering is right by construction, and tests can read results straight after submit.
  • The command reader and the 3D class are plain data code, tested without a graphics card.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• The CPU waits for the GPU on every submit, so real games will need the game's done-signals decoupled from the host's.
  • An acquire that waits for a later release fails instead of waiting.
  • Command lists that use macros fail until the GPU's macro processor, MME64, is emulated.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
core/src/tests/gpu/fifo.rs for decoding and ordering, and the engine tests for report sizes, semaphore values and acquires in emulated RAM.

Sources: core/src/gpu/fifo.rs, core/src/gpu/threed.rs, core/src/gpu/engine.rs.

docs.title: Use the desktop instruction table for the T239 target
In plain words
docs.text: We target Ampere machine code for the T239 with the instruction table of NVIDIA's desktop Ampere chips. We checked inside NVIDIA's own disassembler: its tables for the desktop SM86 chip and the SM88 target are byte for byte the same. Recordings made on a desktop card validate the translator against real Ampere silicon, but no Switch 2 shader or hardware has been tested.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The decoder is generated from the SM86 table, the desktop Ampere instruction set. The Switch 2's chip, the T239, has a GA10F GPU, which CUDA calls SM88. If its encodings differed, every handler keyed on SM86 would be wrong in places.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Keep the SM86 table. NVIDIA's disassembler, nvdisasm, accepts --binary SM88, and its built-in tables for SM86, SM87 and SM88 are byte-identical.

Compared with the committed table Result CUDA version checked 13.1 Encoding classes, the table's rows None added or removed Bit fields None changed Decoder keys None changed Opcode names Some marked internal, which would break the generated handler names Every fixture word Disassembles the same under SM86 and SM88

NVIDIA's public open-gpu-doc headers also list the T239 under the same 3D class as the desktop GA102 family.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Recordings from a desktop GA102 card check the SM86 encodings used by the translator.
  • Handler names stay the public, readable opcode names.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text: • Behaviour is only checked on desktop chips, so equality on a Switch 2 is assumed.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The extracted SM88 table is kept on gpu/sm88-table beside a diff summary; regenerate and diff it when a new CUDA ships.

Sources: scripts/sm_86_instructions.txt, scripts/decoder_generator.rs, CUDA 13.1 nvdisasm, open-gpu-doc classes/3d.

docs.title: Real chips are the reference, and known differences are listed per device
In plain words
docs.text: No public document says exactly what every Ampere instruction does. So we ask the chip. We run one instruction on a rented desktop Ampere card, record its inputs and outputs, and require the translator to give the same bytes. Where a Vulkan driver is known to differ, the exception is written down by name, for that driver only.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: There is no trustworthy public SM86 assembler and no complete description of what instructions do. Hand-built encodings have been wrong before. Public docs and other emulators cover Maxwell, an older NVIDIA generation, not Ampere. Vulkan drivers also differ in float rounding, denormals (tiny near-zero floats) and NaNs (not-a-number results).

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Results are checked against registers read back from real Ampere cards. A capture patches one instruction word into a seed kernel, a small CUDA program built with nvcc that carries the instruction. It runs through the CUDA driver and records inputs and outputs. Observed results are never typed in by hand, and every word is checked with nvdisasm first.

Scoreboard tests replay every capture on each device and fail on any mismatch not listed. Allowed mismatches are listed by fixture id with a reason, either for every device or for lavapipe only.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• It finds bugs no reading of documentation would, such as NaN rules, tensor rounding and shuffle clamping.
  • A device quirk cannot hide a translator bug, because the quirk is excused for that device only.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Each session needs a rented card and some seeds crash, so coverage arrives in batches.
  • The recordings come from desktop GA102 cards, not from a Switch 2.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
fixtures_match_silicon, fixtures_match_warp_silicon and fixtures_match_tensor_silicon pass on Intel and lavapipe.

Sources: core/tests/fixtures/README, core/src/tests/gpu/fixtures.rs.

docs.title: Command processor and memory
docs.text: The command processor is the GPU's front desk: it reads a program's command lists and hands each command to the right engine. Memory follows one rule: the emulated RAM holds the only real copy of anything. For example, if a program moves a vertex buffer, the next draw reads the new place, because every copy is checked against RAM.

docs.title: What does a command look like?
docs.text:
A program puts commands in a pushbuffer, a list of 32-bit words in emulated RAM. It then adds an entry to the GPFIFO, a ring of pointers to those lists. Each command starts with a header word saying which register to write, on which engine, and how many data words follow.

Item Bits Meaning GPFIFO entry word 0 31:2 Pushbuffer address, low part GPFIFO entry word 1 7:0, 9, 30:10, 31 Address high byte, level, length in words, sync Header 11:0 Method, the register to write, as a word index Header 15:13 Subchannel, the slot that picks the engine Header 28:16 How many data words follow, or the value itself in immediate mode Header 31:29 Mode: 1 incrementing, 3 non-incrementing, 4 immediate, 5 increment once, 7 end of segment

Low method numbers belong to the channel, the command stream itself. Its SET_OBJECT binds an engine, a class, to a subchannel, and its SEMAPHORE_A to D methods write "got this far" signals. Every other method goes to the class bound on the header's subchannel. An empty subchannel or an unknown class is an error.

flowchart LR
    GP["GPFIFO entry<br/>Pointer to a command list"] --> PB["Pushbuffer words<br/>Headers and data"]
    PB --> HDR{"Channel method?<br/>Number below 0x40"}
    HDR -->|"Yes"| CH["Channel<br/>Bind engines, write signals"]
    HDR -->|"No"| SUB{"Which engine is on the subchannel?"}
    SUB -->|"0xC797"| TD["3D engine registers<br/>Frozen per draw"]
    SUB -->|"0xC7C0"| CC["Compute engine<br/>Reads the launch block and runs it"]
    SUB -->|"Other"| ERR["Named error"]

How one command word finds the engine it is meant for.

docs.title: What does the 3D engine keep?
docs.text:
The 3D class, 0xC797, is the drawing engine. ThreeD keeps its raw register words and notes which groups changed: vertex streams, attributes, colour targets, viewport and scissor, shaders, constant buffer bindings, blend and depth, and the index buffer.

At each draw it freezes a DrawSnapshot, a copy of everything the draw needs. That covers the triangle type, counts and instances, vertex streams and attributes, and every shader slot. It also holds the first colour target, the depth target, viewport, scissor, write mask, culling and blending. The index buffer, the bound constant buffers and the texture and sampler pools are in it too.

Two more things happen at a draw:

  • A draw framed by BEGIN that continues the previous one with the next instances merges into one instanced draw. Instancing means drawing the same mesh many times in one call.
  • The window origin setting says whether screen y counts up from the bottom row, and whether triangles flip which side faces forward. The snapshot carries both, and the engine flips the picture to match.

A constant buffer, or cbuf, is a small read-only table the game hands a shader, such as the camera matrix. LOAD_CONSTANT_BUFFER updates one, and it is an ordered event too. So a cbuf changed between draws reaches the right draw.

docs.title: How is a compute launch read?
docs.text:
The compute class, 0xC7C0, starts compute work. A launch is described by a QMD, a fixed-size block in emulated RAM. Writing SEND_SIGNALING_PCAS_B makes the class fetch the QMD at SEND_PCAS_A and decode it into a DispatchSnapshot. The engine then runs it, see the GPU pipeline.

QMD field group What it holds Program The shader's address Grid and block How many thread groups, and how many threads per group Memory Shared memory size, shared and local memory windows Constant buffers Eight cbuf bindings Signals Two release semaphores Limits Barrier and register counts Textures The sampler and texture pools Version QMDV02_03 and QMDV03_00; others are rejected

docs.title: How do GPU addresses become memory?
docs.text:
Shaders use GPU virtual addresses (VA), which the game can point anywhere. PageMap turns them into physical offsets in emulated RAM. There is one map per GPU address space, and an address outside it is an error, never a guess.

MemoryTracker stamps every write to a physical page with a global counter, the generation, and who wrote it, CPU or GPU. A host copy compares that counter with the one it was made from, so it knows when it is stale.

Fact Value Page size 64 KiB, the big page size Ryujinx uses; the T239 value is unverified Map scope One per GPU address space Host copy Keyed by Refreshed when Buffer mirror: vertices, cbufs Physical RAM ranges The ranges' generation moved Render target, the image a draw paints Ranges, format, size, depth Loaded before a draw when its pages changed elsewhere, always written back after Texture Ranges, texture header, sampler entry The ranges' generation moved Depth target The draw's depth address Kept on the host only; it must be cleared before its first draw Translated shader Hash of shader header and code Never, the key is the content

The rule: emulated RAM is the authority. Every GPU result is written back before submit returns. A colour target whose pages changed outside its own draws is loaded from RAM before the next draw. A clear that no draw uses is written into RAM, where the next draw loads it. So drawing into an image and then sampling it as a texture shows the latest draw. Repointing a VA changes what the next draw reads.

Why: keying by physical page stays right when memory is remapped or shared. Nothing can show a frame the emulated RAM does not hold. See ADR-0004.

docs.title: What do semaphores and reports write?
docs.text:
A semaphore release writes a value to memory, so the CPU can see how far the GPU got. A report is the same kind of write, asked for by the 3D class. An acquire is the other side: it waits until a memory word reaches a value.

Command What lands in emulated RAM Semaphore release One 32-bit word Short report One 32-bit word Full report The 64-bit value and a 64-bit timestamp in nanoseconds Acquire Nothing; it is checked against the word in memory

Commands run one after another here, so nothing else could release a waiting acquire. An acquire is therefore checked at once, and one that is not already met is a named error.

docs.text:

The cores and GPU use the same GuestRam mapping. A turn lock prevents simultaneous access. Writes to GPU-backed ranges mark pages dirty; the engine refreshes only those pages before it runs. GPU results are downloaded before the CPU resumes.

The kernel catches SVC, dispatches it outside the CPU lock and resumes with a result. It owns the handle table, memory regions, IPC sessions, events, threads, timers and scheduler. Unsupported calls return an error rather than silent success.

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
CUDA is NVIDIA's way of writing general programs for its GPUs. Programs compiled for a desktop sm_86 Ampere card give the translator independent compiler input and can be checked on real NVIDIA silicon. For example, the project builds NVIDIA's Mandelbrot sample source into one of its own demos and runs it through the translator.

The emulator runs compiled CUDA programs through the translator, on any Vulkan device. It can also run them natively on an NVIDIA card through libcuda, NVIDIA's driver library.

    CUBIN --> LOAD["Kernel::load<br/>Finds code, constants, shared size"]
    LOAD --> LAUNCH["Kernel::launch<br/>Fills constant buffer 0 like the driver"]
    LAUNCH --> TR["Translator + Vulkan<br/>Any graphics card"]
    SASS["Ampere machine code"] --> WR["Seed cubin writer<br/>Wraps the code as a CUDA program"]

Both ways a compiled CUDA program runs, and the byte comparison between them.

docs.title: How does the cubin runner work?
docs.text:
A kernel is one CUDA program, and a cubin is the ELF file nvcc, NVIDIA's compiler, puts it in. Kernel::load reads the kernel's code, info, constant and shared-memory sections. It takes the chip version from the ELF header, accepts sm_80 to sm_89 only, and finds where the kernel's parameters go.

Kernel::launch fills constant buffer 0, the small read-only table every kernel gets, the way the CUDA driver does:

Offset in cbuf0 Holds Note 0x0 Block dimensions Threads per group in x, y, z 0xc Grid dimensions Groups in x, y, z 0x28 Initial stack pointer for R1 The real card gives a driver address; here the top of the translator's local array 0x118 Memory descriptor Zero on the card, zero here 0x160 on Kernel parameters Offsets and sizes from the cubin's EIATTR_KPARAM_INFO Section read Holds .text.<kernel> The machine code .nv.info.<kernel> Parameter layout, from EIATTR_PARAM_CBANK and EIATTR_KPARAM_INFO .nv.constant<bank> Constant data .nv.shared.<kernel> Shared memory size

Why this layout: it was recorded from the real driver on a real card. So a cubin compiled today runs without patching.

docs.title: How does the native path work?
docs.text:
cuda.rs, behind the cuda cargo feature, wraps a shader in a cubin made from a small seed kernel. It swaps in the code, parameter area, shared size, instruction offsets and metadata, and keeps the seed's ELF header and segments.

It opens libcuda.so.1 at run time, with no new crate. Then it initialises CUDA, makes a context, loads the module, launches it and waits. CudaDevice::run_native copies buffers in and out.

When it applies: a host with an NVIDIA card and driver that load sm_86 cubins, running compute programs. The translator stays the reference and the portable path, and the native tests check both give the same bytes. Graphics shaders never run natively.

docs.title: What this does and does not show
docs.text:
oboromi emulates the hardware: an AArch64 CPU, an Ampere GPU, display and an audio DSP path. The GPU translator is validated against desktop sm_86 NVIDIA silicon. Command and shader-header layouts come from NVIDIA's published headers via Mesa.

Nintendo supplies the OS; oboromi does not emulate it. The small service layer in this repository is a stand-in that lets our own test programs drive the emulated GPU, display and audio. It follows Switch 1 interfaces because those are known.

Every demo is our own program built with our SDK. No Switch 2 binary, shader, firmware or exploit was used, and no retail or third-party binary has run. The demos show the hardware emulation running end to end with code written for it, not Switch 2 software compatibility.

docs.title: GPU pipeline
docs.text: A program draws by writing a list of commands into memory and telling the GPU where the list is. The emulator reads that list, collects the settings for each draw, rewrites its Ampere machine code for Vulkan, and draws on the PC's graphics card. For example, a triangle takes a handful of commands: where the shaders are, where the vertices are, the viewport, then "draw".

docs.title: How does a draw reach Vulkan?
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant RAM as Emulated RAM
    participant P as Pusher (reads command lists)
    participant C as 3D class (drawing registers)
    participant E as Engine
    participant T as Translator (SASS to SPIR-V)
    participant V as Vulkan (PC graphics card)
    E->>P: Queue of command lists
    P->>RAM: Fetch command words
    P->>C: Register writes
    C-->>P: Frozen draw settings
    P-->>E: Events, in command order
    E->>RAM: Read shader header and code
    E->>T: NVIDIA shader code
    T-->>E: Vulkan shader
    E->>RAM: Copy the buffers the draw reads
    E->>V: Build pipeline, draw
    V-->>E: Pixels
    E->>RAM: Write pixels back
    Note over E,RAM: The display reads the finished image from emulated RAM

One draw, from the program's command list to pixels back in emulated memory.

The words on this path:

  • A pushbuffer is one command list in emulated RAM, and the GPFIFO is the queue of pointers to those lists.
  • A method is one command: a write to a GPU engine's register.
  • The 3D class is the drawing engine's register set.
  • SASS is NVIDIA's shader machine code, and SPIR-V is the shader format Vulkan accepts.
  • A Vulkan pipeline bundles the shaders with the settings Vulkan must know before drawing.

docs.title: What happens at each step?
docs.text: Step Code Output Read queue entries and command headers fifo.rs Pusher::submit Register writes, each aimed at one engine Bind engines to slots, run channel commands fifo.rs channel Semaphore events, the GPU's "I got this far" signals Keep the drawing registers, freeze them at each draw threed.rs ThreeD::write Event::Draw(DrawSnapshot) Read the shader header (SPH) and code, translate engine.rs module, sm86 translate_program SPIR-V, cached by a hash of header and code Copy the buffers the draw reads engine.rs mirror PC-side buffers, keyed by where they sit in emulated RAM Run compute launches engine.rs dispatch Emulated RAM pages the program changed Draw and read back graphics.rs VkState::draw RGBA8 pixels Write back and show engine.rs draw, present Emulated RAM, then display::present

docs.title: Why does submit wait for every draw?
docs.text: Gpu::submit returns only after every draw has landed in emulated RAM. So any later CPU read sees the result, with no extra waiting. See ADR-0006.

docs.title: Why freeze the settings at each draw?
docs.text: A draw must see the registers as they were when it was issued. The frozen copy, the snapshot, keeps later commands from changing a draw that is still running.

docs.title: Does compute work take the same road?
docs.text:
Yes, through the compute class 0xC7C0. A QMD, the block in emulated RAM that describes one compute launch, becomes a dispatch snapshot (see command processor). The engine translates the program, runs it over the mapped memory window, writes back changed pages and releases the launch's semaphores.

Verified by: the engine tests in core/src/tests/gpu/engine.rs on Intel and lavapipe (Mesa's CPU-based Vulkan driver), with the Vulkan validation layer reporting no errors. They cover the pushbuffer triangle with a vertex remap and a QMD compute launch. They also cover indexed, instanced, depth-tested, blended and textured draws, render to texture, clears, reports, acquires and both y-flips.

Sources: core/src/gpu/{fifo,threed,engine,graphics}.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/engine.rs.

docs.title: Emulator path
docs.text:
The included demos are the project's own no_std AArch64 images. The loader places an image in emulated RAM, starts it on the emulated CPU and lets it drive the hardware through a small stand-in service layer. That layer follows known Switch 1 interfaces; Nintendo's OS is not emulated.

flowchart TB

    K --> NV["GPU driver services"]
    K --> AU["Audio services"]
    K --> VI["Display services"]
    NV --> GPU["GPU engine"]
    GPU --> RAM[("Emulated RAM")]
    VI --> WIN["Qt window"]
    AU --> OUT["Qt audio output"]
    P --- RAM

The images use the aarch64-unknown-none target and are built by scripts/build-guest.sh. Shared encoders in the scene crate build command lists, shader headers, texture headers and demo data without duplicating the oracle path.

docs.title: Emulator overview
docs.text:
oboromi builds on a Rust core, a Qt front end, emulated ARM cores, a stand-in service registry, an NVIDIA instruction table and a SPIR-V writer. The current path connects those foundations into one machine: the loader starts one of the project's AArch64 images, the kernel handles its calls, the stand-in services drive graphics and audio, and the window presents the result. Nintendo's OS is not emulated.

docs.text:
An image loaded by the emulator calls the GPU driver stand-ins, writes commands into emulated RAM and submits them. The GPU engine translates the Ampere machine code, runs it through Vulkan and writes the result back. The display stand-in queues that buffer, then display::present notifies the Qt window.

The same route runs the Dungeon, ray-traced BoomBox, Mandelbrot precision dive, solar-system birth and the smaller demos. Tests may call lower layers directly as oracles, but the demo buttons use the emulator path.

No retail or third-party binary has run. No Switch 2 binary, shader or firmware was used to build this path.

Verified by: the loader, kernel, service, audio and GPU suites, plus the fixed-frame demo tests in core/src/guest.rs.

docs.title: Hardware-backed limits
docs.text:
The translator is checked against desktop sm_86 Ampere silicon. NVIDIA's SM86 and SM88 instruction tables are byte-identical, but no Switch 2 shader has been seen and no code here has been validated on a physical Switch 2.

FOOTPRINT fields have been measured on SM86, while its complete raw result and portable Vulkan mapping remain open. BAR.SCAN runs only with a full-warp count in the tested forms, but its result was not observable through the documented barrier readers. Those instructions therefore remain named failures instead of guessed implementations.

Verified by: the subsystem suites named on each architecture page, the CUDA corpus probe and the silicon fixture scoreboards.

Sources: core/src/cpu, core/src/kernel, core/src/nn, core/src/audio, core/src/gpu, guest, scene.

docs.title: SASS translator
docs.text: Ampere GPUs run NVIDIA machine code called SASS, which an Intel or AMD card cannot run. The translator rewrites each SASS program into SPIR-V, the shader format every Vulkan driver accepts. For example, FADD R0, R1, R2 becomes "load the source registers from an array, add them as floats, store the sum".

docs.title: How are instructions decoded?
docs.text:
A generator reads the instruction table NVIDIA's disassembler, nvdisasm, carries, and writes the decoder as Rust code. Each row of that table, an encoding class, becomes one branch of the decoder. Each branch calls a handler, the function that emits SPIR-V for one instruction family.

Decoder fact Value Instruction word 128 bits, scheduling bits included Decoder key Bit 91 plus bits 11:0 Generator scripts/decoder_generator.rs reads scripts/sm_86_instructions.txt Output sm86_decoder_generated.rs Alternate-syntax classes Skipped, so a shorthand never hides the real instruction Unknown word Panics

Why the translator uses the SM86 table for its Switch 2 target: NVIDIA's disassembler ships byte-identical tables for SM86 and SM88. No Switch 2 shader has been used to validate that choice. See ADR-0007.

docs.title: Where does the emulated GPU state live?
docs.text:
SPIR-V has no direct way to name the emulated GPU's hardware registers. Each register therefore becomes an entry in an array the shader owns. "Private" below means one copy per thread, and "Workgroup" means one copy shared by a group of threads.

Emulated state Home in SPIR-V Note Registers R0 to R253, RZ Private array of 32-bit words RZ always reads zero Predicates P0 to P6, PT One Private word of bits One-bit "run this?" flags; PT is always true Uniform registers UR0 to UR62, UP The same array, after the predicates Values shared by a whole warp Live flag Last word of the array Finished threads start past the end pc, return addresses, BSSY tokens B0 to B15 Private variables The program position and the rejoin markers Local memory Private array 4 KiB per thread Shared memory Workgroup array 1 KiB per workgroup Warp exchange, schedule slots Workgroup arrays Where threads swap values and vote

docs.title: How do jumps work without goto?
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    start["pc = 0<br/>Start of the program"] --> loop{"Is the pc still inside the program?"}
    loop -->|"No"| done["Return"]
    loop -->|"Yes"| sw["Jump table on pc<br/>One entry per straight run of code"]
    sw --> blk["Run that piece of code;<br/>A branch just sets the next pc"]
    blk --> loop

The fallback turns machine-code jumps into one loop around a jump table.

Vulkan only accepts structured control flow: nested loops and ifs, never a free jump. The Beyond Relooper structurizer now turns reducible machine-code control flow into nested SPIR-V selections and loops. Programs it cannot structure use the pc dispatcher shown above, where a branch stores the next program position and one loop runs the matching block.

Those pieces are basic blocks, runs of code with no jump in or out except at the ends. A block starts at the program start, at every jump target, after every branch and EXIT, at BSYNC and after BAR. A jump to an address held in a register (BRX, JMX, CALL) could land anywhere, so then every instruction starts a block. EXIT sets the pc past the end.

An instruction with a predicate, such as @P0 FADD, is wrapped in an if on that predicate. Uniform instructions check their uniform predicate instead.

docs.title: What happens when threads of a warp disagree?
docs.text:
A warp is the team of threads the chip runs in lockstep. When teammates take different sides of a branch, that is called divergence. Most programs never need teammates to meet again, so each thread simply runs its own pc loop.

Some instructions do need every teammate at the same place, because they swap values or wait for each other. Examples are VOTE, SHFL and BAR. A program that uses any of them runs in turns. In each turn, the threads furthest behind, those at the lowest pc, run one block. Threads at other pcs sit that turn out.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
This program adds one on even threads only, then swaps a value with the next thread:

Block Code A Set a flag for even threads; odd threads jump to C B Add one to R1 C SHFL: read R1 from the next thread, then EXIT Turn Even threads wait at Odd threads wait at Who runs 1 A A Everyone runs A; even threads go on to B, odd threads jump to C 2 B C B is lower, so even threads run it; odd threads wait 3 C C Everyone runs C together, so every swap sees the updated R1

Without turns, odd threads would reach the swap first and read R1 before their even teammates had added one.

docs.title: The details
docs.text:
• The instructions that make a program run in turns: VOTE, SHFL, MATCH, REDUX, BAR, the tensor instructions, LDSM, MOVM and R2UR.OR.
  • Swapped values travel through a shared array, with a barrier before and after.
  • A thread that waits sits its turn out, and its memory writes are masked.
  • BSSY gives each thread a token for where it should rejoin; BSYNC waits while a teammate holding the same token is still elsewhere.
  • BAR counts arrivals per barrier and lets the threads go once all have arrived.
  • A program that can never make progress marks itself stuck, and the test harness panics.

Why turns: every thread of a group must reach a Vulkan barrier together. And on lavapipe, Vulkan's own subgroups are narrower than a warp, so they cannot stand in for one. See ADR-0003.

docs.title: Which slots does a shader read its data from?
docs.text:
A Vulkan shader cannot follow pointers to its data. It reads from numbered slots, called bindings, and the host plugs a buffer or image into each slot before the run. A group of slots is a descriptor set. Compute and vertex shaders use set 0, and pixel shaders use set 1 with the same numbers.

Binding Kind Holds 0 Uniform buffer, small and read-only oboromi's own helper values, never game data 1 to 32 Uniform buffers The game's constant buffers 0 to 31, stored as uvec4 arrays 33 Storage buffer, large and read-write The window onto emulated RAM 34, 35 Storage buffers Register values in and out, tests only 36 and up Texture and image slots Textures and writable images, in the order the shader first uses them

A constant buffer, or cbuf, is a small read-only table the game hands the shader, such as the camera matrix. Vulkan's std140 layout rule pads every uniform array element to a fixed width. A uvec4 fills that width exactly, so nothing is wasted.

Layout fact Value std140 array element Padded to 16 bytes uvec4 Four 32-bit words, 16 bytes

Stage Translator form Stage-only instructions Compute Stage::Compute { local_size } None Vertex Stage::Vertex ALD and AST, attribute load and store Fragment Stage::Fragment { flat, screen_linear, depth } IPA, attribute interpolation

docs.title: Textures and tensors
docs.text: Some instructions need more than a direct rewrite. Texture reads need a program's image descriptions turned into Vulkan images. Tensor core instructions, which multiply small matrices in one go, need Ampere's own way of adding numbers for bit-exact results. Exact mode uses that method; the default uses the faster cooperative path.

docs.title: How does a shader find its texture?
docs.text:
A texture is an image a shader reads with filtering, and a sampler holds the reading settings, such as edge wrapping. A program describes both in tables in emulated RAM, called pools. The TIC pool holds texture headers (format, size, layout, address) and the TSC pool holds sampler entries.

The shader picks one entry from each pool with a handle, one word stored in a constant buffer (cbuf). The translator records where each handle comes from, as a cbuf bank and byte offset. Each distinct source gets its own Vulkan slot, a binding, numbered upwards from 36. Before the run, the PC reads the handle, decodes both pool entries, and plugs in a Vulkan image with its sampler. The image is uploaded again whenever its emulated pages change, so a texture that was drawn into shows its latest draw. In draws, textures are read by pixel shaders today.

Handle bits Picks Low 20 The TIC entry, the texture Top 12 The TSC entry, the sampler, unless the game links each sampler to its texture's index 
flowchart LR
    CB["Handle word<br/>In a constant buffer"] --> TIC["Texture header<br/>Format, size, layout, mip levels"]
    CB --> TSC["Sampler entry<br/>Edge wrap, filtering, detail level"]
    TIC --> DET{"How are the pixels laid out?"}
    DET -->|"Plain rows"| PL["Copy rows as they are<br/>One level"]
    DET -->|"NVIDIA tiles"| BL["Untangle the tiles<br/>Per mip level"]
    PL --> IMG["Vulkan image"]
    BL --> IMG
    TSC --> SMP["Vulkan sampler"]
    IMG --> BIND["Texture slot<br/>Binding 12 and up"]
    SMP --> BIND

How one handle word becomes a Vulkan image and sampler in a shader slot.

docs.title: Which textures are supported?
docs.text:
Decoded Supported Layouts Plain rows (pitch-linear) with one level; NVIDIA tiles (block-linear) with a chain of mip levels Formats A8B8G8R8 UNORM and sRGB, R8, G8R8, R16G16B16A16 float, R32 UINT, compressed BC1, BC3, BC7 Type and channel order 2D, channels in their normal order Sampler Repeat or clamp to edge, nearest or linear filtering, mip filter and detail clamp Rejected by name Other formats, channel orders and types, depth compare, anisotropy, reduction filters, unnormalized sampler coordinates

A mip level is a smaller copy of the texture, used when it is far away. sRGB is a colour encoding that matches how screens show brightness.

docs.title: What is a block-linear texture?
docs.text:
Block-linear is NVIDIA's tiled layout. It keeps pixels that are close on screen close in memory, which makes reads faster. The tiles are GOBs, groups of bytes, and GOBs stack into taller blocks. The decoder untangles the tiles back into rows.

Block-linear fact Value GOB size 64 bytes wide, 8 rows high Inside a GOB 16-byte pieces, interleaved Blocks GOBs stacked along Y Block height per mip level Shrinks as the level shrinks, the way Ryujinx's size calculator does

docs.title: Which instructions read textures?
docs.text:
Instructions Vulkan form TEX, TLD, TLD4, TXD, TXQ, TMML: sampled reads and queries Combined image samplers SULD, SUST, SURED, SUATOM: pixel loads, stores and atomics Storage images

TMML asks which mip level a read would use. In compute it gets its slopes from Vulkan's compute-shader derivative groups.

Why record where the handle comes from, not its value: the source is known when translating, but the value is only known at run time. A handle whose source cannot be traced fails by name.

docs.title: How are matrix instructions run?
docs.text:
Tensor core instructions (HMMA, IMMA, DMMA, BMMA, LDSM and MOVM) compute D = A × B + C on small matrices. The matrices are spread across a warp, the team of threads that runs in lockstep. Each thread holds a few elements, its matrix fragment. The translator runs them per thread and shares each input register through one exchange array.

Layout fact Value Which thread holds what Thread 4g + t holds row g of a fragment Sharing Each source register goes through one warp exchange

docs.title: How does the chip add the products?
docs.text:
Standard float maths adds one number at a time and rounds after each step. The real chip does not sum HMMA products that way. Exact mode reproduces its method bit for bit:

Step Rule Grouping Products in groups of 8 along k (4 for TF32); C joins the group sum Alignment Every term is lined up to the largest exponent; a product's exponent is ea + eb Truncation Bits below 2^(emax-24) are dropped, not rounded Sum Exact integer sum, turned back into f32 by truncation .F16 result Each group rounds to f16 Inf and NaN Standard float rules, applied to only the special terms

docs.title: Why is the sum written as loops?
docs.text:
Written straight out, the exact method makes a huge shader that drivers take long to compile. Putting it in one SPIR-V function did not help, because both drivers pasted it back into every caller. So the inputs are loaded once into a per-thread array. The sum runs in loops marked DontUnroll, a hint that tells the driver to keep each loop as a loop. OBOROMI_EXACT=1 selects this path. See ADR-0005.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Each translated instruction has to prove it behaves like the real chip. The strongest proof is running the instruction on a real Ampere card and comparing every output byte. For example, one instruction runs on a rented RTX 3090 with known inputs. The translated version must then give the same bits on Intel and on lavapipe.

docs.title: Which checks exist?
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    T1["1. spirv-val<br/>Every Vulkan shader we write is well formed"] --> T2["2. nvdisasm<br/>Every hand-built instruction word is the one we meant"]
    T2 --> T3["3. silicon captures<br/>Results match a real RTX 3090 or A6000"]
    T3 --> T4["4. compiled programs<br/>Real CUDA programs give the right output end to end"]

The checks, from cheapest to most convincing.

A handler, the code that translates one instruction family, is not done until it passes every check that applies. It must pass on Intel and on lavapipe, Mesa's CPU-based Vulkan driver.

Oracle and digest tests select exact mode explicitly. The normal emulator defaults to speed hacks; OBOROMI_EXACT=1 or SpeedHacks::none() disables them.

docs.title: How are silicon captures made?
docs.text:
A capture patches one instruction word into a small compiled CUDA program, the seed kernel. It runs that program on an NVIDIA Ampere card through the CUDA driver and reads the registers and memory back. The capture machine uses the NVIDIA driver for exact SASS. The word is built from the instruction table and checked with nvdisasm before the run.

The result is stored as a fixture: the word, the inputs, the outputs, and whether the result was really observed. Observed results are never typed in by hand.
